stemMd:
Art historian Livia Okonjo attributes the unsigned altarpiece in the chapel of Santa Brigida to the painter Maestro Anselmo himself rather than to one of his pupils. She cites two kinds of evidence: the pigments match those in Anselmo's signed panels, and infrared imaging reveals an underdrawing with the loose, rapid hatching seen in his other work. ______ the pigment match proves less than it first appears to, since Anselmo's workshop bought its colors in bulk and shared them among all its painters. It is the underdrawing, which no pupil is known to have imitated, that carries Okonjo's case.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
explanationMd:
Decide first whether the blank's sentence helps or hurts the argument being reported. Okonjo offers two pieces of evidence for Anselmo. The blank's sentence then says one of them, the pigment match, is weak: every painter in the workshop used the same colors, so a match would appear whoever painted the panel. The final sentence falls back on the other piece of evidence, the underdrawing.

A writer who grants a weakness in a case while still holding to the case is making a concession, and **Admittedly** is the transition that marks one. It tells the reader "this point counts against the argument, and I accept it" before the text returns to the evidence that survives.

The trap is to read the blank's sentence as more detail about the pigments, because it continues the pigment topic from the sentence before. Topic is not the test; direction is. Check by asking whether the sentence makes Okonjo's case stronger or weaker. It makes it weaker, so any transition that adds, confirms, concludes or compares in the same direction is wrong, and only a concession fits.

distractorRationale.d: This introduces a point that confirms or strengthens what came before. The sentence does the reverse: it tells the reader that the pigment evidence is weaker than it looked. A reader who picks this has followed the topic (pigments again) instead of the direction of the argument.
distractorRationale.c: This presents the sentence as a conclusion drawn from the evidence just listed. Nothing in the evidence implies that the pigment match is weak; that follows from a new fact, the shared workshop supplies, which the sentence itself introduces.
distractorRationale.a: This signals a second point parallel to the first. The sentence is not another piece of evidence like the pigments and the underdrawing; it is an objection to one of them.

accessibilityText: Four sentences about an unsigned altarpiece, with a blank at the start of the third. The first says art historian Livia Okonjo attributes the altarpiece to Maestro Anselmo rather than to a pupil. The second says she cites two kinds of evidence: matching pigments, and an underdrawing whose hatching resembles his other work. The third says the pigment match proves less than it first appears to, because the workshop bought colors in bulk and shared them among all its painters. The fourth says the underdrawing, which no pupil is known to have imitated, carries her case. Choose the transition for the blank from Similarly, Admittedly, Thus, and Indeed.

provenance.notes: Original item. The altarpiece, the chapel of Santa Brigida, Maestro Anselmo and Livia Okonjo are invented; no source text was adapted.

review.author: wave7-sat-rw-expression-conventions-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The writer concedes that one of Okonjo's two pieces of evidence is weak, because pigments were shared across the workshop. The writer then says the underdrawing carries the case. That is a concession, so 'Admittedly' fits. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave7-sat-rw-run1) reached the same answer: The writer concedes a weakness in one half of Okonjo's evidence, then says the other half carries her case, which is a concession. 'Admittedly' fits. 'Indeed' and 'Thus' wrongly present the weakness as reinforcing or following from what came before, and 'Similarly' draws no parallel here.]

review.notes: Author's own solve and uniqueness check: The blank's sentence weakens one of Okonjo's two pieces of evidence while the passage still upholds her attribution, so the relation is concession; only 'Admittedly' marks it. 'Indeed' confirms, 'Thus' concludes, 'Similarly' parallels; each would require the sentence to support her case. 'However' and 'Still' were deliberately excluded because a plain contrast word could also be defended. Re-solved from the stem alone: same answer. Unique. STRETCH: harder than a typical hard transitions item because the blank's sentence continues the topic of the previous sentence (pigments) while reversing its argumentative direction, so the topic cue points to the confirming distractor; the key is an attitude marker (a writer conceding a weakness in a reported case) rather than a plain logical connector, and no generic contrast word is offered as a shortcut. The candidate must track whose case is being argued across four sentences. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
